newsitem.title: PERU: More Peru hostage talks as rebel leader said grim.
newsitem.headline: More Peru hostage talks as rebel leader said grim.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages in Lima began a sixth round of talks with the government on Tuesday as a source close to doctors attending captives said the rebel leader's mood was darkening.

A white Red Cross car carried Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) representatives from the besieged Japanese ambassador's home to a safe house across the street for talks with government negotiator, Domingo Palermo.
Rebels staying behind saw off the car with now traditional shouts of defiance, yelling out "We will never surrender."

The three guarantors of the talks -- from the Vatican, the Red Cross and the Canadian government -- also crossed police lines and drove to the meeting, which began at about 4:15 p.m. local time (2115 GMT).
As negotiations to end the 70-day siege dragged on, word of the state of the hostages and their captors came from a source close to medical teams that regularly enter the residence for check-ups.
The source told Reuters that the hostages were in generally good spirits and health but that Cerpa was increasingly morose.
"Cerpa looks irritated. He doesn't speak with everyone anymore," said the source, who asked not to be named.

But the hostages, especially Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki and Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, were cheerful when the doctors entered the residence after the fourth round of talks with the government last Thursday.

"There is an atmosphere of optimism inside the residence. Some of them play chess, card games, ludo, and others read books so as not to be bored as they wait for whatever is going to happen," said the source.
"Cerpa's attitude has changed in the past few days. Before the meetings he was very talkative, but now he only speaks with ambassador Aoki and Tudela," the source said.
Hostages freed at the beginning of the crisis reported that the Tupac Amaru chief was courteous and approachable, even joining in roundtable discussions on Peruvian politics.
While Cerpa now holds himself aloof from most of the hostages, his relationship with Aoki and Tudela has intensified since negotiations began on Feb. 11.
"Every time a meeting is over, they (Cerpa, Aoki and Tudela) get together and talk," the source said.

The hostages were mostly in good health. But two need to have medicine brought in for serious illnesses. Congressman Gilberto Siura suffers from stomach cancer and former Supreme Court president Moises Pantoja has a heart condition and severe arthritis.
The doctors also examine the rebels if they ask for it.

"Once two of the MRTA women asked the doctors, half joking but half seriously, if they could do a scan to see if they were pregnant," the source said. "Anyway, they did the tests and they were negative."

The 15-odd heavily armed guerrillas seized the residence during a coctail party to celebrate the Japanese emperor's birthday on Dec. 17. Their chief demand is the freeing of 400 jailed comrades and their hostages include President Alberto Fujimori's brother, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two government ministers.
